title: Maple's three RateLimitIDs show the inflow/outflow abstraction breaks down for asynchronous redemption
content:
Every other instance's `Rate Limit IDs` document speaks of "this conduit's inflow and outflow" — two legs. The Maple USDT instance (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.3.2.2.3) instead lists three keyed hashes: `deposit`, `withdraw` and `redeem`.

The reason surfaces in the same instance's `Instance-specific Operational Parameters` (.3.2.4), which exists to hold "operational parameters or configuration details unique to this Instance that deviate from or otherwise supplement the general Spark Liquidity Layer parameters", and whose only child is `Request Redemption Parameters` (.3.2.4.1): "`maxAmount`: Unlimited, `slope`: 500,000,000 USDT per day".

Maple exits are asynchronous — a redemption is *requested*, queued, and settled later — so the single moment the inflow/outflow model assumes does not exist. `withdraw` and `redeem` are different actions with different failure modes, and the act of requesting redemption needs its own throttle distinct from both.

The consequence for the Artifact's structure is that the two-leg `Inflow Rate Limits` / `Outflow Rate Limits` schema is not a general model of a conduit; it is a model of synchronous pool deposits that happens to fit most venues. Where a protocol's lifecycle has more states, the limits spill out of the standard slots into instance-specific parameters — and a reader who only consults the standard slots will miss a 500,000,000 USDT per day throttle entirely.
description: The Maple USDT instance publishes distinct deposit, withdraw and redeem limit IDs, so a two-legged template must describe a three-action protocol where exit is a request, not an immediate transfer.
